Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters Sheikh Hasina Exiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threat Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students Penelope MacRae in Delhi Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.45 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Bangladesh’s ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence. “They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government. Hasina, 78, who has lived under tight security in India since fleeing Dhaka, said on Wednesday she would return in December – Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, marking the defeat of Pakistani forces in the 1971 war of independence. “Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people,” the former Awami League leader told a news conference at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi, speaking via audio link. View image in fullscreen Sheikh Hasina, the then newly elected prime minister, speaking at a press conference in Dhaka in January 2024. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters Her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, told the news conference she was being treated well in exile. “She is staying with the full services and security of a head of state,” he said. “Prime minister [Narendra] Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect, and for that I am eternally grateful.” The exiled Awami league members plotting a political comeback in Bangladesh – from India Read more India officially distanced itself from the news conference, saying it had no role in organising it and did not endorse the political views expressed. India has been walking a diplomatic tightrope over Hasina, who was one of its closest regional allies. Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since her downfall and India has been seeking to mend relations with Bangladesh while resisting demands for her extradition. Hasina’s flight ended more than 15 years of increasingly authoritarian Awami League rule. The Bangladesh Nationalist party, led by Tarique Rahman, the son of the former prime minister Khaleda Zia, swept to power earlier this year in an election that barred the Awami League. The government has said Hasina would probably be arrested the moment she set foot in Bangladesh. View image in fullscreen Sajeeb Wazed Joy, the son of Sheikh Hasina, addressing the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia on Wednesday via video link. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters Last November, Bangladesh’s international crimes tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the violent suppression of the protests. The demonstrations began over government-job quotas and snowballed into a mass movement against Hasina’s government. The UN estimates up to 1,400 people may have died. Hasina’s supporters say the death toll was about 800. She has rejected the court’s verdict as politically motivated and said the execution threat would not change her plans. Hasina was imprisoned several times during her fierce rivalry with Zia, who died in 2025. The two women traded claims of using corruption cases and arrests against each other in a “Battle of the Begums”, an honorific title for a senior woman. View image in fullscreen Sheikh Hasina, right, and her former political foe, Khaleda Zia, at a wedding reception in Bangladesh in 1997. Photograph: Reuters Bangladesh has prohibited domestic media from broadcasting or publishing Hasina’s statements. She has demanded that the ban on the Awami League be lifted, political prisoners be released and “false cases” against party activists be dropped. Claiming Bangladesh is sinking into lawlessness and economic ruin, she accuses the new government of trying to erase the country’s secular character. The government has been grappling with high inflation and sluggish economic growth while blaming many of the country’s problems on alleged corruption and mismanagement during Hasina’s years in power. Photograph: Dariusz Borowicz/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Reuters Europe ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank Report warns attacks on critical infrastructure could lead to demand for retaliation and expose EU divisions Jon Henley Europe correspondent Fri 27 Nov 2026 09.46 EST Last modified on Fri 27 Nov 2026 10.50 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian sabotage attacks on Europe are increasing and a “mass-casualty event” is now possible as increasingly skilled operatives target critical infrastructure with ever more complex methods, a leading strategic thinktank has said. The International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report that Russian intelligence services and their proxies were targeting European railways, energy networks and defence industries in an attempt to weaken support for Ukraine. Russian sabotage had risen by 16% in 12 months and the use of arson and explosive devices had doubled, the IISS said, “presenting a risk of mass-casualty incident … as the space for miscalculation narrows”, and of subsequent retaliation and escalation. While unskilled ⁠recruits were still carrying out most operations, a semi-skilled tier of operatives were now using more intricate methods, ​including improvised explosive devices with ‌timed and remote detonators, the report said. National authorities across Europe had arrested proxies, expelled intelligence officers and sometimes closed Russian consulates, but there was “no clear evidence that these measures have made sabotage a less attractive instrument of Kremlin policy”. “Arrests remove ‌proxies, but are highly unlikely to deter the Russian intelligence services that direct ‌them,” it said, with attacks by “layers of intermediaries” coming “in surges, concentrated on strategically important countries and sectors”. The IISS said Germany and Poland would remain the most targeted states, as their transport and industrial networks were crucial to supplying Ukraine. Targeting of critical infrastructure accounted for more than half of incidents over the past 12 months. The report said 29 Moscow-linked incidents were recorded in Poland between October 2025 and September 2026, including a November 2025 incident in which an explosive charge damaged a railway line used for delivering supplies to Ukraine. In Leipzig, Germany, on 4 August, a drone laden with explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used for military supplies. Investigators ‌suspect a second drone collided with a DHL cargo plane soon after air traffic was suspended. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Russian national charged with spying on Silicon Valley tech and defense firm Read more The IISS said the key question facing Europe was whether it could turn a series of national decisions in response to specific incidents into a Europe-wide strategy before “an operation conducted by the RIS [Russian intelligence services] or proxies causes a mass-casualty event”. An operation that caused fatalities or serious disruption would “generate demands for retaliation” and could expose divisions between EU governments, it said, with none having set red lines despite recent attacks in Estonia , Lithuania and Romania. The possibility of a mass-casualty attack – whether deliberate or by miscalculation – raises “concern about escalation [being] the primary instinct”, the IISS said, calling for Europe to “publicly signal what level of harm triggers which response”. Moscow has rejected out of hand all accusations from western governments and intelligence services that it is behind a Europe-wide campaign of drone, cyber, arson and explosive attacks aimed at undermining and disrupting EU support for Ukraine.
